claims.text: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr is a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The engineered alloy has an inverted microstructure consisting of a continuous disordered BCC matrix and discrete nanoscale B2 precipitates.
The inverted Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr alloy will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition as temperature increases.
The alloy will be ductile at both low and high temperatures but brittle over a narrow intermediate-temperature range.
Casting, hot isostatic pressing, and homogenization produce an initial microstructure with a continuous ordered B2 matrix and discrete BCC precipitates.
The initial ordered-B2-matrix condition is brittle.
Solutionizing at 1400 °C followed by water quenching and annealing at 600 °C for 120 hours produces the inverted BCC-matrix/B2-precipitate microstructure.
The discrete B2 precipitates are approximately 50 nm in size.
The B2 precipitates are hard obstacles to dislocation motion.
At low temperature, the disordered BCC matrix permits ample dislocation motion and therefore high ductility.
Around 600 °C, B2 precipitates become especially effective at pinning dislocations.
Dislocation pinning by B2 precipitates around 600 °C creates stress concentrations that sharply reduce ductility.
At temperatures near 800 °C, thermal activation overcomes the precipitate barriers and restores dislocation mobility and ductility.
The alloy will exhibit a marked reduction in fracture strain near 600 °C relative to room temperature and approximately 800 °C.
The brittle temperature window may be accompanied by anomalous strengthening.
Conventional alloys such as tempered steels typically exhibit temper embrittlement.
High-entropy alloys generally do not exhibit temper-embrittlement-like behavior unless their microstructure is deliberately engineered.
The brittle-state temperature range depends on the volume fraction, size, and spacing of the B2 precipitates.
Processing variations and strain rate may shift the transition temperature or change the magnitude of the ductility loss.
